pages.title: Logical Address Space
pages.content:
- In this submodule, we’ll explore a foundational concept in memory management — **Logical Address Space**. This is how the operating system views and manages memory for running programs.
- Just like how a map provides symbolic locations (not actual terrain), logical addresses act as abstract references used by a program, independent of actual physical memory locations.



---

**What is Logical Address Space?**
**Logical Address Space** (LAS) refers to the set of addresses generated by a program (usually by the CPU during execution). These addresses are not the actual memory locations in RAM but symbolic ones used during code execution.

**Note:**The CPU generates **logical addresses**, which are later mapped to **physical addresses** by the **Memory Management Unit** (MMU).

---

**Key Concepts**
| Term | Description |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Logical Address** | The address generated by the CPU. Also called Virtual Address. |
| **Address Space** | The range of addresses a process can use. |
| **MMU** | A hardware unit that translates logical addresses to physical addresses at runtime. |

**Real-Life Analogy**
- Imagine you order a package using your name and street address (e.g., "John, 12 Rose Lane"). This is like a **logical address** — easy for you to use.



- But internally, the delivery system uses a **GPS coordinate** (latitude/longitude) to route the package. That’s the **physical address**.

**Why Use Logical Address Space?**
- **Abstraction:** Programs don’t need to worry about real memory layout.
- **Security:** Processes can't directly access other program's memory.
- **Flexibility:** OS can move programs around in physical memory without changing their logical addresses.
- **Portability:** Code can run on different machines without changing address values.

---

The **Logical Address Space** is a key abstraction used by modern operating systems to manage memory efficiently and securely. It allows the CPU and programs to operate using symbolic addresses, leaving the actual memory translation to the MMU.

In the next section, we’ll dive deeper into **Physical Address Space**, the real location in memory where data is stored.

pages.title: Physical Address Space
pages.content:
- Now that we've understood how **Logical Address Space** (LAS) works as a symbolic memory abstraction for programs, it's time to explore the **real memory locations** where data is actually stored — the **Physical Address Space** (PAS).
- Just like a GPS coordinate pinpoints an exact location on Earth, physical addresses refer to **concrete memory cells** in the system’s RAM.

---

**What is Physical Address Space?**
- Physical Address Space refers to the **set of all actual memory addresses** in the system’s **main memory** (RAM) that a process may occupy after address translation.
- When a program runs, the CPU generates **logical addresses**, but these are **translated by the MMU (Memory Management Unit)** into **physical addresses** before accessing RAM.

**Note:**
The **physical address** is invisible to the running program. The OS and hardware handle this translation seamlessly.

---

**Key Concepts:**
| Term | Description |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Physical Address** | The actual memory location in RAM where data or instructions are stored. |
| **Physical Address Space** | The complete range of real memory locations available in RAM. |
| **MMU (Memory Management Unit)** | Hardware that maps logical addresses to physical addresses. |

**How Logical → Physical Mapping Works:**
1. CPU generates a **logical address** (e.g., 0x00001234)
2. MMU translates it to a **physical address** (e.g., 0xFA120234)
3. RAM is accessed at that exact **physical location**



This process allows:
- Relocation of processes in memory
- Security via isolation of address spaces
- Efficient memory management

---

**Why Physical Address Space Matters:**
- It's the **real memory** that holds actual data and instructions.
- Determines the **RAM capacity limit** of the system.
- Impacts performance and memory allocation decisions.
- Important for low-level operations like **paging**, **segmentation**, and **cache management**.

**Difference Between Logical & Physical Address:**



| **Feature** | **Logical Address** | **Physical Address** |
| --------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------ |
| Generated By | CPU | MMU (via translation) |
| Visibility | Visible to the program | Not visible to the program |
| Resides In | Logical Address Space | Physical Address Space (RAM) |
| Portability | Code remains portable | Tied to actual memory hardware |
| Can Be Modified | Easily relocated by OS | Fixed once allocated |

---

- The **Physical Address** Space is the real memory backbone of any system. Every instruction, variable, and data structure must eventually reside in this address space to be executed or used.
- While **logical addresses** provide abstraction and flexibility, physical addresses anchor everything to real hardware.

pages.title: Fixed Partitioning - Contiguous Memory Allocation
pages.content:
After learning about **logical and physical address spaces**, it’s time to understand how memory is actually allocated to processes. One of the oldest and simplest techniques used in early operating systems is **Fixed Partitioning**.

**What is Fixed Partitioning?**
- Fixed Partitioning is a **contiguous memory allocation** technique where the main memory (RAM) is divided into **fixed-size blocks** or **partitions** at system startup. Each partition can hold exactly **one process at a time**, and once defined, the **partition sizes do not change** during runtime.



- Think of it like dividing a bookshelf into fixed compartments, each meant to hold one book. Regardless of the book's size, it must fit into one of those predefined compartments.

---

**Types of Fixed Partitioning:**
There are two main types:
1. **Equal-Sized Partitions**

- All partitions are the same size.
- Simple to implement.



2. **Unequal-Sized Partitions**

- Partitions are of varying sizes.
- More flexible but needs a smart allocation strategy.

**Drawbacks: Fragmentation Issues:**
- **Internal Fragmentation:**
If a process doesn't use the entire partition space, the leftover memory inside that partition is wasted.

- **Limited Number of Processes:**
The number of partitions limits the number of processes that can be in memory at once, even if free space exists.

---

**Example:**
Suppose your RAM is 16 KB, divided into 4 fixed partitions of 4 KB each.
- Process A (2 KB) is assigned a 4 KB partition → 2 KB wasted
- Process B (4 KB) is assigned a 4 KB partition → no waste
- Process C (5 KB) → **can’t be loaded**, even though total free space = 10 KB!



**Characteristics Summary:**
| **Feature** | **Description** |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| Partition Size | Fixed at system start |
| Number of Processes | Limited by number of partitions |
| Fragmentation Type | Internal fragmentation |
| Flexibility | Very low (static design) |
| Simplicity | Very simple to implement and manage |

---

**Why Study Fixed Partitioning?**
Even though it’s obsolete in modern systems, Fixed Partitioning forms the **basis for understanding more advanced memory allocation schemes** like dynamic partitioning, paging, and segmentation.

**Fixed Partitioning** is a simple memory allocation method that divides RAM into static blocks. While easy to manage, it leads to poor memory utilization in dynamic environments.

pages.title: Variable Partitioning
pages.content:
After learning Fixed Partitioning, where memory is divided into fixed-size blocks, let’s now explore a more flexible approach: **Variable Partitioning**.

**What is Variable Partitioning?**
- Variable Partitioning is a **contiguous memory allocation** technique where memory is divided **dynamically** based on the size of incoming processes, instead of pre-fixed blocks.
- **Analogy:** Imagine a flexible shelf where each new book gets a custom-sized compartment, exactly matching its size—no predefined gaps!



**How it Works:**
- When a process arrives, it is allocated **just enough memory**.
- Memory is **split dynamically** to match the size of the process.
- Once the process finishes, that memory space is freed and can be reused.



---

**Advantages of Variable Partitioning:**
- **Efficient Memory Use:** Memory is allocated exactly as needed.
- **No Internal Wastage:** No leftover space inside a partition since there's no fixed block size.
- **Dynamic Design:** It adapts to different process sizes easily.

**Drawbacks of Variable Partitioning:**
- **Memory Gaps Over Time:** As processes enter and leave, free memory might become scattered in small chunks.



- **Rearranging Needed:** The OS may occasionally need to rearrange memory **(compaction)** to better accommodate new processes—this takes time.
 Think of it like clearing space in your backpack: sometimes you have to shuffle things around to fit a new item.

---

**Compaction:**
- To improve memory usage, the OS may **shift processes together**, creating one large free area. This process is called **compaction**.
- Imagine sliding all apps on your phone’s home screen to one side to free up space for a widget.



**Variable vs Fixed Partitioning:**
| **Feature** | **Fixed Partitioning** | **Variable Partitioning** |
| ---------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------- |
| Partition Size | Fixed | Dynamic (based on process size) |
| Space Efficiency | Low (can waste memory) | High (only needed space allocated) |
| Flexibility | Rigid | Flexible |
| OS Complexity | Simple | Slightly complex (due to shifting) |

---

**Variable Partitioning** allocates memory blocks based on process size, avoiding the limitations of fixed partitions. While more efficient, it introduces challenges like **scattered memory**, which require smart memory management techniques such as **compaction**.

pages.title: Internal Fragmentation
pages.content:
- After learning **Fixed** and **Variable Partitioning**, it’s important to understand a common problem that can arise in memory allocation: **Internal Fragmentation**.
- Internal Fragmentation occurs when **allocated memory** is slightly **larger than the memory actually requested by the process**.



- As a result, a small amount of memory inside the allocated block is **left unused**, and this wasted space is called **internal fragmentation**.

**Analogy:**
- Imagine reserving a **hotel room** that has two beds, but you're a solo traveler. You only need one bed, but you're forced to pay for the whole room.
- That **extra bed** is like internal fragmentation—memory that’s allocated but not used.



---

**Why Does It Happen?**
- **Mostly occurs in Fixed Partitioning**, where memory blocks are of fixed size.
- If a process needs 3.6 KB, and the nearest available block is 4 KB, the remaining 0.4 KB goes unused.
- Over time, these small gaps **add up**, reducing overall memory efficiency.

**Characteristics of Internal Fragmentation:**
- Happens **inside** the allocated partition.
- Wasted memory is **not reusable** unless the whole block is freed.
- More noticeable when **block sizes** are large and **process sizes** vary a lot.

---

**Example:**
| **Memory Block Size** | **Process Size** | **Internal Fragmentation** |
| ----------------- | ------------ | ---------------------- |
| 4 KB | 3.5 KB | 0.5 KB |
| 8 KB | 7.2 KB | 0.8 KB |

Even though the process is loaded successfully, the unused portion inside the block is **internal waste**.

---

**When is Internal Fragmentation Less Likely?**
- In **Variable Partitioning**, memory is allocated exactly as per process size — so internal fragmentation is **almost eliminated**.
- Using **Smaller Fixed Block Sizes** can also reduce the waste, but increases the number of partitions to manage.

**Drawbacks of Internal Fragmentation**
- Reduces **effective memory utilization**
- Difficult to track and recover this wasted space
- Can lead to **denial of service** if enough memory is locked in small, unusable chunks.

---

**Internal Fragmentation** is the unused memory **within an allocated block** caused when memory is given in **fixed-sized units**, and the process doesn’t use it all.
It’s a common problem in **Fixed Partitioning** and is minimized in **Variable Partitioning** where memory is allocated more precisely.

pages.title: External Fragmentation
pages.content:
- After learning about **Internal Fragmentation**, where wasted space exists *inside* an allocated block, it's time to understand another common memory problem — **External Fragmentation**.
- **External Fragmentation** occurs when the **total free memory is enough to satisfy a request**, but the free blocks are **scattered and non-contiguous**.



- As a result, **no single block** is large enough to fulfill the process request — **even though** the sum of all free spaces is sufficient.

**Analogy:**
Imagine a hotel has **5 vacant rooms**, but none are adjacent.
A family wants **3 connected rooms** but can't be accommodated — even though the total space is available.
This scattering of free space is like **external fragmentation**.



---

**Why Does It Happen?**
- Happens mostly in **Variable Partitioning**, where blocks of memory are created dynamically as needed.
- When processes complete and are removed, **gaps** are left in memory.
- Over time, these gaps add up and cause **fragmentation** outside of allocated blocks.

**Characteristics of External Fragmentation:**
- Wasted space exists **outside allocated blocks**.
- Total memory is enough — but **not in a single continuous chunk**.
- Occurs due to **frequent allocation and deallocation** of processes.
- Makes it difficult to find a big enough block for large processes.

---

**Example:**
```default
Total Memory: 16 KB
Free Blocks: [2 KB] [1 KB] [4 KB] [3 KB] = 10 KB free
Process Request: 6 KB
```
- Total free = 10 KB
- But no single block ≥ 6 KB → Request **fails** due to external fragmentation.

---

**How to Reduce External Fragmentation?**
1. **Compaction**
- Shifts processes together in memory to **combine scattered free spaces**.
- Requires **processes to be relocatable**.
- Often used in OSes that support dynamic memory movement.

2. **Paging or Segmentation**
- Instead of allocating contiguous blocks, memory is split into **equal** or **logical** units.
- These eliminate or drastically reduce external fragmentation.

**Key Differences (vs. Internal Fragmentation):**



| **Feature** | **Internal Fragmentation** | **External Fragmentation** |
| ----------------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Location of waste | Inside allocated block | Outside allocated block |
| Common in | Fixed Partitioning | Variable Partitioning |
| Can be solved by | Precise allocation | Compaction / Paging |

**External Fragmentation** is the result of scattered free memory blocks that are individually too small to fulfill larger memory requests.
It mainly occurs in **Variable Partitioning**, and solutions like **compaction** and **paging** are used to reduce or eliminate it.
We will learn about **paging** in detail later in this course.

pages.title: Paging Concepts - Basics of Paging
pages.content:
- Paging is a **memory management technique** used by operating systems to manage memory efficiently and flexibly.
- It eliminates the need for contiguous allocation and solves several problems seen in older techniques.

**Why Use Paging?**
Traditional memory management (like contiguous allocation) often leads to external fragmentation and inefficient memory use.
Paging solves this by:
- Dividing memory into **fixed-size** blocks
- **Loading only required parts** of a program into memory
- Supporting **non-contiguous allocation** of program memory



---

**Key Terminology**
| **Term** | **Description** |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| **Page** | A fixed-size block of a program (logical memory) |
| **Frame** | A fixed-size block in RAM (physical memory) |
| **Logical Address** | The address generated by the CPU or program |
| **Physical Address** | The actual address in RAM where data is stored |
| **Page Table** | A data structure that maps pages to frames (explained next in KP2) |




**Advantages of Paging**
- Removes **external fragmentation**
- Allows **non-contiguous memory allocation**
- Makes efficient use of RAM

---

In the next section, we'll explore how the mapping between pages and frames is managed and how address translation works efficiently using the Page Table.

pages.title: Paging Concepts - Page Tables
pages.content:
- **Page Tables** are essential for managing the mapping between a program’s **logical memory** (pages) and **physical memory** (frames).
- Every time a program accesses memory, the operating system uses the **Page Table** to translate logical addresses into physical addresses.

**Why Are Page Tables Needed?**
- When a program runs, it uses **logical addresses**. These addresses don’t directly point to physical memory.
- To access the correct **frame** in RAM, the OS needs a way to know **where each page is stored** - that’s exactly what the **Page Table** does.

---

**Address Translation with Page Tables:**
1. Software is divided into equal-sized pages.
2. RAM is divided into equal-sized slots (called frames).
3. Pages are loaded into any available slot in RAM.
4. When a program uses a logical address:
- The OS figures out **which page** it belongs to.
- Finds the **frame number** from the page table.
- Combines frame number + offset to get the **physical address**.

**Example:**
Let’s say:

- Page Size = 1024 bytes
- Logical Address = 2050

---

**Step 1: Break the Address**
```sdf
Page Number = 2050 / 1024 = 2
Offset = 2050 % 1024 = 2
```

---

**Step 2: Use Page Table**
```sd
Page 2 is stored in Frame 5
```

---

**Step 3: Calculate Final Address**
```sdf
Physical Address = (5 × 1024) + 2 = 5122
```
---

**Structure of a Page Table:**


| **Page Number** | **Frame Number** |
| ----------- | ------------ |
| 0 | 5 |
| 1 | 12 |
| 2 | 10 |
| 4 | 8 |
| 5 | 2 |

**Key Characteristics:**
- **Each process** has its **own Page Table**.
- Stored in **main memory**, accessed during each memory reference.
- Can become **large** in systems with **big address spaces**.

**Limitation of Page Tables:**
- Looking up the page table **takes extra time**.
- Large tables **consume memory**.
- That's why operating systems use Translation Lookaside Buffer (**will discuss in next knowledge point**).

---

**Page Tables** are crucial in a paging system as they map each page of a program's logical memory to a specific frame in physical memory. This mapping allows the operating system to translate **logical addresses** into **physical addresses** during program execution, ensuring accurate memory access.

pages.title: Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)
pages.content:
Now that you understand how a **Page Table** helps translate logical addresses to physical addresses, let's address one major limitation:
- Every memory access requires **two steps**: first, access the **page table** (in RAM), then access the actual **memory location**.
- This can **slow down performance**, especially in systems with large page tables.

That’s where **TLB** comes in.

**What is TLB?**
- TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer) is a small, fast **cache** used by the **Memory Management Unit (MMU)** to store **recent page table entries**.
- Think of it as a **shortcut table** that remembers the most recent page-to-frame translations. If the translation for a page is already in the TLB, the system can skip accessing the main page table — making memory access **much faster**.

---

**Real-life Analogy:**
Imagine you're in a library.



- You frequently refer to 2-3 books.
- Instead of walking to the shelves every time (like accessing the main memory), you keep them on your desk (like the TLB) for quick reference.

---

**How TLB Works - Step-by-Step:**
1. CPU **generates a logical address**.
2. The **MMU checks the TLB** to see if it already has the page number's frame.
- **TLB Hit** → Get the frame number directly.
- **TLB Miss** → Go to Page Table in main memory, find the frame number, and update the TLB.
3. Once the frame number is found, **combine it with the offset** to form the physical address.
4. Access the physical memory.



**TLB Hit and Miss:**
| **Term** | **Meaning** |
| ------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **TLB Hit** | The required page number is **found in the TLB**. Very fast address translation. |
| **TLB Miss** | The page number is **not found in the TLB**. The system must access the page table in RAM, then update the TLB. |

**Key Characteristics of TLB:**
- Implemented in **hardware** (unlike Page Table, which is in RAM).
- Stores **only a few entries** (e.g., 16–1024 entries).
- Operates **much faster** than main memory.
- If TLB hit ratio is high (say 95–99%), the system avoids accessing slow main memory most of the time, greatly **boosting overall performance**.

---

**Formula for Effective Memory Access Time (EMAT):**
Let’s assume:
- Memory access time = **100 ns**
- TLB lookup time = **10 ns**
- TLB hit ratio = **80%**

Then,
**EMAT = (Hit Ratio × (TLB access + Memory access)) + (Miss Ratio × (TLB access + 2 × Memory access))**

Substitute:
**EMAT = (0.8 × (10 + 100)) + (0.2 × (10 + 200)) = 88 + 42 = 130 ns**

---

The **Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)** is a fast, hardware-based cache that stores recent page table entries to speed up virtual-to-physical address translation. A higher TLB hit ratio significantly improves performance by avoiding the need to access main memory for page table lookups.

pages.title: Inverted Page Tables
pages.content:
After learning about standard Page Tables and Translation Lookaside Buffers (TLBs), it’s time to explore a more **space-efficient way** to manage virtual memory: the **Inverted Page Table**.

**What is an Inverted Page Table?**
An **Inverted Page Table** (IPT) is a type of page table where **each entry represents a frame in physical memory**, rather than a page in logical memory.
- In traditional paging, every **process has its own page table**, which can consume a lot of memory.
- In **inverted paging**, there's only **one global page table** for the whole system, and it stores **which virtual page (and from which process)** is currently occupying a particular **frame** in physical memory.

---

**How Does Inverted Paging Work?**
Each entry in the Inverted Page Table contains:



- **Process ID** (which process the page belongs to)
- **Virtual Page Number** (the page number in that process’s address space)
- **Control Bits** (valid, protection, etc.)

Address Translation Flow:
1. CPU generates a **virtual address** (contains process ID + page number + offset).
2. The system **searches the IPT** to find a matching (PID + Page Number).
3. If a match is found → retrieve the **physical frame number** and access memory.
4. If not found → **page fault** (page is not in memory).



- **`m`** represents the **number of bits** used for addressing physical frames in physical memory.

---

**Why Use Inverted Page Tables?**
| **Feature** | **Traditional Page Table** | **Inverted Page Table** |
| ------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------- |
| Entries per process | Many (can be huge) | None |
| Total tables | One per process | One for entire system |
| Memory usage | High (per-process tables) | Low (one table, tied to RAM size) |
| Lookup Speed | Fast (with TLB) | Slower (requires searching) |

**Drawbacks of Inverted Paging:**
- **Slower lookups:** Because it may need to search through the entire table.
- **Hashing required:** Many systems use hash tables to speed up the search process.
- **More complex implementation** compared to standard page tables.

**When Are Inverted Page Tables Used?**
- In systems with **very large address spaces**, such as 64-bit machines.
- When memory overhead from traditional per-process page tables becomes too costly.
- Examples include some **Unix-like OS kernels and modern mainframes**.

---

An **Inverted Page Table** is a memory-efficient structure that maps **frames to virtual pages**, reversing the traditional approach of mapping pages to frames.

pages.title: Basics of Segmentation - Memory Management
pages.content:
- After understanding **paging**, where memory is split into blocks, let’s now explore another memory management technique that's **closer to how programs are actually structured: Segmentation**.
- **Segmentation** is a memory management scheme that divides a process into **logically meaningful**, **variable-sized units** called **segments**.

These segments represent different parts of a program, such as:



- **Code** (instructions)
- **Data** (global/static variables)
- **Stack** (function calls, local variables)
- **Heap** (dynamically allocated memory)

Instead of slicing memory into uniform pieces like paging, segmentation divides it **based on the program's logical structure**.

---

**Real-Life Analogy:**
- Think of a **bookshelf** where each shelf holds a different category—**fiction**, **science**, **history**—and each shelf is sized to fit its books.



- That’s segmentation: memory is divided into logical, variable-sized sections, just like the shelves.

**Why Use Segmentation?**
- Reflects **how programmers view memory**
- Allows **logical grouping** of program components
- Provides **flexibility**, since each segment can grow or shrink independently

---

**Logical Address Format in Segmentation:**
In segmentation, each memory reference is made using:
```default
Logical Address = (Segment Number, Offset)
```
- **Segment Number:** Identifies which segment (e.g., code, data)
- **Offset:** Position within that segment

The OS will later use this pair to locate the actual data in RAM — this process is called **address translation**, which we’ll cover after we learn about segment tables.

---

**Example:**
Let’s say a program has:
| **Segment Number** | **Segment Name** | **Size (in bytes)** |
| -------------- | ------------ | --------------- |
| 0 | Code | 1000 bytes |
| 1 | Data | 500 bytes |
| 2 | Stack | 300 bytes |



A logical address like (1, 250) means:
- `1` → **Segment Number** (i.e., Data segment)
- `250` → **Offset** within that segment

**What it means:**
You're asking the system to access the **250th byte inside the Data segment**.

This address would be translated into a physical address using a **segment table** (will cover in the next knowledge point).

---

**Key Features of Segmentation**
- Memory is divided based on **logical sections** of a program.
- Segments are **not equal in size**.
- Each segment is accessed independently.

pages.title: Segment Table - Memory Management
pages.content:
Now that you've learned that a **logical address in segmentation** is made up of a (**Segment Number**, **Offset**) pair, it's time to understand **how the system keeps track of each segment**.

This is where the **Segment Table** comes in.

**What is a Segment Table?**
- A Segment Table is a **data structure** used by the **Operating System** to keep track of **each segment’s location** and **size in physical memory**.
- Each **process** has its own Segment Table, created and maintained by the OS.
- It enables the OS to manage and protect different parts of a program like **code**, **data**, **stack**, and **heap** independently.

---

**Structure of a Segment Table:**
Each entry in a Segment Table represents a **segment** and contains the following fields:



| **Field** | **Description** |
| ---------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Base** | The **starting physical address** where the segment is stored in RAM. |
| **Limit** | The **length (size)** of the segment in bytes. |
| *(Optional)* Protection Bits | Used by OS to control segment access (read/write/execute permissions). |

These fields help the OS manage **which segment is where** in RAM and how much space it occupies.

---

**Example Segment Table:**
Let’s say a program has the following segment table:
| **Segment Number** | **Segment Name** | **Base (in RAM)** | **Limit (Size)** |
| -------------- | ------------ | ------------- | ------------ |
| 0 | Code | 1000 | 1000 bytes |
| 1 | Data | 2000 | 500 bytes |
| 2 | Stack | 3000 | 300 bytes |



This table tells the OS that:
- The **code** segment starts at memory location **1000** and is **1000** bytes long.
- The **data** segment starts at **2000**, and is **500** bytes long.
- The **stack** segment starts at **3000**, and is **300** bytes long.

This information will be used for address translation in the **next knowledge point**.

---

**Key Features of Segment Table:**
- Each **process** gets its own segment table.
- Enables **logical separation** of different program parts (code, data, stack).
- Allows **modular memory allocation** and better **access control**.
- Helps enforce **memory protection** (e.g., you can make code segment read-only).

A **Segment Table** holds the **base and size of each segment** in a process. It helps the OS manage segmented memory more efficiently and safely by tracking **where each segment begins and how large it is**.

pages.title: Concept of Virtual Memory - Memory Management
pages.content:
- After learning about **paging** and **segmentation**, you might wonder — what happens when a program is **larger than** the available physical memory (RAM)?
- This is where **Virtual Memory** steps in — allowing programs to run as if the system has **more RAM than it physically does**.



---

**What is Virtual Memory?**
- Virtual Memory is a **memory management technique** that gives the illusion of a large, continuous main memory to processes, even if the actual physical memory is limited.
- It allows programs to **execute even if their entire code/data is not loaded** into RAM all at once.

**Key Idea:**
- Instead of loading the entire program into memory, only the **required parts (pages/segments)** are loaded **on demand**, while the rest stay on the **disk (secondary storage)**.
- The OS handles this seamless movement of data between **RAM** and **disk**.

---

**Real-Life Analogy:**
- Imagine your **study table (RAM)** is small, but your **bookshelf (Disk)** is huge.
- You don’t need all your books on the table at once—you only keep what you're currently reading.
- When needed, you swap books in and out.
- That’s how **Virtual Memory** works!



---

**How Does Virtual Memory Work?**
1. Each process gets its **own** virtual address space.
2. The OS and hardware (MMU) **map virtual addresses to physical addresses** using page tables (with help from TLB).
3. Only the **needed pages** are kept in RAM.
4. If a required page is not in RAM **→ Page Fault** occurs → OS fetches it from disk and updates memory.

**Key Benefits:**
| **Feature** | **Description** |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Larger program execution** | Programs larger than RAM can run easily. |
| **Process isolation** | Each process gets its own virtual memory space → Better security. |
| **Efficient memory use** | Only necessary data stays in RAM, rest swapped to disk. |
| **Multitasking** | Multiple programs can run efficiently, each in its own virtual space. |

**Where is Virtual Memory Stored?**



- **Physical Memory (RAM):** Holds active parts of processes.
- **Backing Store (Disk):** Stores inactive parts of programs temporarily.
- OS uses **swap space or page file** on disk to manage this.

**Common Terms:**
| **Term** | **Meaning** |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Page** | A fixed-size block of virtual memory. |
| **Frame** | A fixed-size block of physical memory (RAM). |
| **Page Fault** | When a page is not in RAM and must be loaded from disk. |
| **Backing Store** | Secondary storage used to store pages not in RAM. |

---

**Virtual Memory** enables systems to **run large programs** by using **disk space as an extension of RAM**. It offers better **resource utilization**, **process isolation**, and **multitasking**, making modern computing efficient and scalable.

pages.title: Demand Paging - Virtual Memory Management
pages.content:
- After understanding how **Virtual Memory** allows programs to run without fully loading into RAM, it’s time to learn **how and when data** is actually brought into memory. This is where **Demand Paging** comes in.
- **Demand Paging** is a **lazy-loading** memory management technique where **pages are loaded into RAM only when they are needed**, not before.



- Instead of loading the entire process into memory during execution, only the **required pages** are brought in on demand.
- If a page is accessed but is not in memory → a **Page Fault** occurs → the OS loads it from disk.

---

**How Demand Paging Works – Step by Step**



1. **Process starts execution**
→ Only minimal pages are loaded initially (e.g., first instruction/page).
2. **CPU accesses a page**
→ MMU checks whether it’s in memory.
3. **If page is in memory**
→ Continue execution normally (**Page Hit**).
4. **If page is NOT in memory**
→ **Page Fault** occurs.
5. **OS handles the Page Fault**
→ Finds the page on disk (backing store) and brings it into a free frame in RAM.
6. **Page Table and TLB are updated**, and the process resumes.

**What is a Page Fault?**
A **Page Fault** is triggered when the CPU accesses a page that is **not currently in RAM**.
- The OS suspends the process.
- Loads the required page from disk.
- Resumes execution once the page is available.



Frequent page faults can degrade performance (called **Thrashing**), so efficient page replacement policies are needed.

---

**Key Features of Demand Paging**
| Feature | Description |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **On-Demand Loading** | Pages are loaded **only when needed** (on demand). |
| **Efficient Memory Use** | RAM holds **only active** pages → Saves memory. |
| **Page Fault Handling** | The OS must handle page faults by bringing in pages from disk. |
| **Supports Virtual Memory** | Works in together with **Virtual Memory** for large process execution. |

**Advantages**
- Saves memory by loading only necessary pages.
- Reduces the startup time of programs.
- Enables running large programs on limited RAM.

**Disadvantages**
- Page faults may introduce a **delay** during execution.
- Excessive page faults may cause **thrashing**.

---

**Demand Paging** is a smart memory-saving technique where **pages are brought into RAM only when needed**, not all at once. It relies on **page faults** to fetch data from disk and works seamlessly with **Virtual Memory** to support large, multi-tasking systems efficiently.

pages.title: FIFO Page Replacement Algorithm
pages.content:
**FIFO** stands for **First-In, First-Out** — it’s one of the simplest page replacement algorithms.

Think of it like a **queue**: the page that was loaded first is the one that gets removed first when memory is full.

---

Imagine your computer can hold only **3 pages in memory at a time**. If a new page comes in and memory is full, FIFO removes the **oldest** page - even if it's still needed!

- It’s like a backpack that can hold 3 books. When you want to add a new book and the bag is full, you remove the one you packed first.

| ---- | ------- | ------------- | ----------------- |
| 1 | 7 | \[7] | Yes |
| 2 | 0 | \[7, 0] | Yes |
| 3 | 1 | \[7, 0, 1] | Yes |
| 4 | 2 | \[0, 1, 2] | Yes (7 removed) |
| 5 | 0 | \[0, 1, 2] | No |
| 6 | 3 | \[1, 2, 3] | Yes (0 removed) |

* A **page fault** occurs when the page isn’t in memory.
* If memory is full, FIFO removes the page that came in first.
* It doesn’t care whether the page is still useful — it’s just first-in, first-out.

pages.title: LRU - Page Replacement Algorithm
pages.content:
**LRU** stands for **Least Recently Used**.

- When your memory is full and a new page needs to be loaded, LRU removes the page that **hasn’t been used for the longest time** — the “least recently used” one.


- Think of it like switching between apps on your phone. If your phone can keep only 3 apps running, and you haven't used App A in a while, it’ll be the first one to be cleared when you open a new app. That’s LRU in action.

---

Let’s say you have **3 memory frames**, and the following pages are requested:

```xfxv
Page requests: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4
```

We’ll load pages into memory one by one, tracking which pages were recently used.

| Step | Request | Memory (LRU order → right is most recent) | Page Fault? |
| ---- | ------- | ----------------------------------------- | ----------- |
| 1 | 7 | \[7] | Yes |
| 2 | 0 | \[7, 0] | Yes |
| 3 | 1 | \[7, 0, 1] | Yes |
| 4 | 2 | \[0, 1, 2] (7 removed) | Yes |
| 5 | 0 | \[1, 2, 0] (0 reused → moved to recent) | No |
| 6 | 3 | \[2, 0, 3] (1 removed) | Yes |
| 7 | 0 | \[2, 3, 0] | No |
| 8 | 4 | \[3, 0, 4] (2 removed) | Yes |


**Total Page Faults:** `6`\
**Pages that were reused (no fault):** `0` on step 5 and 7

---

**Summary**

* LRU tracks **how recently each page was used**.
* When memory is full, it removes the page that **hasn’t been used for the longest time**.
* It performs better than FIFO in many real-world situations because it considers usage history.

pages.title: Optimal Page Replacement Algo
pages.content:
- The **Optimal Page Replacement Algorithm** (OPT) is the most efficient page replacement strategy — but with a catch: it's not practically implementable for real-time use.
- In OPT, **when a page needs to be replaced**, the algorithm removes the **page that will not be used for the longest time in the future**.
- It’s like having a magical crystal ball that tells the OS exactly which page won’t be needed soon, so that one gets removed!

---

**Real-Life Analogy:**
Imagine you’re packing for a trip and your bag has limited space. If you somehow know that you won’t wear your black jeans until the last day of the trip, you can safely pack them at the bottom or even leave them out.



That’s what OPT does—it removes the page that won't be used for the longest time ahead.

---

**Example:**
Let’s say we have **3 memory frames**, and the following **page requests** arrive:
**`Page requests: 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4`**

We’ll apply OPT and track page faults.
| **Step** | **Request** | **Memory Frames** | **Page Fault?** | **Action Taken** |
| ---- | ------- | ------------- | ----------- | -------------------------- |
| 1 | 7 | \[7] | Yes | Loaded 7 |
| 2 | 0 | \[7, 0] | Yes | Loaded 0 |
| 3 | 1 | \[7, 0, 1] | Yes | Loaded 1 |
| 4 | 2 | \[0, 1, 2] | Yes | 7 removed (used latest) |
| 5 | 0 | \[0, 1, 2] | No | Already in memory |
| 6 | 3 | \[0, 2, 3] | Yes | 1 removed (used farthest) |
| 7 | 0 | \[0, 2, 3] | No | Already in memory |
| 8 | 4 | \[0, 3, 4] | Yes | 2 removed (not used again) |

- **Total Page Faults: 6**
- **Better than** FIFO and LRU for the same input

---

**OPT** replaces the page that will **not** be used for the **longest time** in the future. It gives the **lowest possible number** of page faults.

**Not practical in real systems** because the OS cannot predict future requests. It is used as a benchmark to compare how other algorithms perform.

practiceProblems.title: LRU Visualization
practiceProblems.description:
**Walkthrough Example**

1. **Generate a Process**:
 - Creates 16 virtual pages (only 8 can be in physical memory at once)
 - Initially, all pages are marked as not present
 - All "last used" timestamps are initialized to -1

2. **Access Pages**:
 - First 8 accesses will cause **page faults** as pages are loaded into empty frames
 - Each access updates that page's "last used" timestamp
 - Subsequent accesses to loaded pages will be **page hits** and update timestamps
 - The 9th access will:
 - Identify the page with the oldest timestamp
 - Replace that page (after writing to disk if modified)
 - Load the new page with current timestamp

3. **Observing LRU Behavior**:
 - The **page table** shows exact last-used timestamps
 - The replacement always selects the page not used for longest time
 - Frequently used pages tend to stay in memory
 - The **event log** shows which page was replaced and why

---

**Learning Points**

1. **Temporal Locality**: LRU exploits that recently used pages are likely to be used again
2. **Perfect LRU vs Approximations**: Real systems often use approximations
3. **Timestamp Overhead**: True LRU requires maintaining exact usage times
4. **Stack Property**: LRU doesn't suffer from Belady's anomaly

The visualization makes these LRU-specific concepts clear by showing:
- Exact timestamps for each page access
- How the replacement choice is made based on usage history
- Why some pages remain in memory while others get replaced
- The relationship between access patterns and page faults

practiceProblems.title: Optimal Visualization
practiceProblems.description:
**Walkthrough Example**

1. **Input a Page Reference String:**
- The user provides a sequence of page requests (e.g., `7,0,1,2,0,3,0,4`) through a text input.
- The user also specifies the number of **available memory frames** (e.g., 3 frames).

2. **Simulate OPT Algorithm:**
- The simulation processes the page requests **step-by-step**.
- If a requested page is **already in memory**, it is a **page hit**.
- If the page is **not in memory**, a **page fault** occurs:
 - If there is free space in the memory frames, the page is added.
 - Otherwise, the page that will **not be used for the longest time in the future** is replaced (this is the core idea of the **Optimal algorithm**).

3. **Observing OPT Behavior:**
- A **step-wise table** shows:
 - The **current page request**
 - The **state of memory frames**
 - Whether it caused a **hit** or a **page fault**
- Rows with hits are highlighted in green (`.hit`), and faults in red (`.fault`).
- At the end of the simulation, you get:
 - **Total Page Faults**
 - **Total Page Hits**
 - **Hit Ratio (%)**

---

**Learning Points:**
1. **Future Knowledge Assumption:** OPT assumes perfect knowledge of future page accesses, which is **not possible in real OS**, but is useful for analysis.
2. **Benchmarking Algorithm:** OPT is used to compare and evaluate the efficiency of real-world algorithms like FIFO and LRU.
3. **Lowest Page Faults:** This algorithm produces the **minimum possible number** of page faults for a given input sequence and frame count.
4. **No Belady’s Anomaly:** Unlike FIFO, OPT **never suffers** from performance anomalies as memory increases.

This Visualization Helps You Understand:
- How **future access patterns** influence page replacement decisions.
- Why **OPT is ideal but impractical** in real operating systems.
- How it performs **better than FIFO and LRU** on the same input sequence.
- The core logic of choosing the page that is **used farthest in the future or is never used again**.

pages.title: Case Study - Memory Management in Linux
pages.content:
- You’ve learned concepts like **paging**, **segmentation**, **virtual memory**, and **page replacement**.
- But how are these ideas actually used in a real operating system like **Linux**? This case study connects the theory to practice - showing how Linux **efficiently manages memory** under the hood using the very techniques you’ve studied.
- Memory management in Linux is the subsystem that controls:
 - How memory is **allocated to processes**,
 - How virtual memory is implemented,
 - And how **pages are swapped in and out** of physical RAM.

Linux uses **paging-based memory management**, along with **virtual memory**, **multi-level page tables**, and a smart **page replacement** strategy.

---

**Key Features:**
1. **Virtual Memory**
- Every process sees its own **private virtual address space**.
- Backed by **demand paging** - physical memory is only allocated when needed.
- Enables programs to run even if they require more memory than available RAM.

2. **Paging and Page Tables**
- Linux uses **paging**, not segmentation, for address translation.
- Memory is divided into **pages** (typically 4KB).
- Each process has its own **page table**.
- Uses **multi-level page tables** to reduce memory overhead.

3. **TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer)**
- A hardware cache for page table entries.
- Reduces the time taken for address translation.
- Automatically maintained by the CPU.

4. **Page Replacement in Linux**
- Linux doesn’t use pure FIFO, LRU, or Optimal.
- Uses a smart approximation of **Least Recently Used** (LRU):
 - Maintains metadata on page usage.
 - **Clock algorithm** (a practical LRU variant) is used.
 - **kswapd:** A kernel thread that reclaims memory when needed.

5. **Swapping and Page Cache**
- When memory runs low, **least-used pages are moved to disk** (swap).
- Frequently accessed files are cached in memory via the **page cache**.
- This improves performance for disk I/O.

---

**Real-World Example:**
Imagine you’re using:
- A web browser,
- A text editor,
- And a terminal window.

Linux handles:
- Page allocation when you open new tabs.
- TLB hits when switching between windows.
- Page replacement when your RAM fills up.
- Swap usage if your system becomes overloaded.

And all of this happens **without crashing your system or slowing you down drastically**.

---

**Summary:**
| **Concept** | **How Linux Uses It** |
| ---------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| Virtual Memory | Every process gets private address space |
| Paging | Used instead of segmentation |
| Page Tables | Multi-level, per-process |
| TLB | Speeds up address translation |
| Page Replacement | Approximate LRU (Clock algorithm) |
| Swapping | Moves least-used pages to disk |
| Page Cache | Keeps frequently used files in RAM |

**Key Takeaways:**
- Linux implements **demand-paged virtual memory** using **multi-level paging**.
- It handles real-time memory pressure via **smart page replacement** and **swapping**.
- Concepts like **TLB**, **LRU**, and **page cache** are used in real, working systems.
